The 5-2 Browns visit the 5-2 Steelers for an AFC North rivalry at Acrisure Stadium, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET on CBS.

setup: The Browns and Steelers renew their AFC North rivalry Sunday at 1 p.m. ET in Pittsburgh with identical 5–2 records. Cleveland won the October 1 meeting 27–24 on Andre Szmyt's 56-yard field goal with 10 seconds left, after Aaron Rodgers erased an 11-point deficit. The rematch shifts to Acrisure Stadium, with Deshaun Watson and Quinshon Judkins trying to keep the Browns on schedule against a Steelers defense eager to force longer downs.

things.title: PITTSBURGH'S PASS RUSH VS. WATSON
things.body: Cleveland's protection has been vulnerable when the offense slips behind schedule. Watson needs quick answers and manageable third downs against a Pittsburgh front that can turn hurried throws into turnovers. In the first meeting, the Browns built their lead by sustaining drives and kept their final possession clean enough to set up the winning kick.

things.title: RODGERS AND METCALF LOOK FOR EXPLOSIVES
things.body: Rodgers threw three touchdowns in the first meeting and DK Metcalf topped 100 receiving yards. Cleveland has to keep Pittsburgh's downfield passing game from creating short scoring drives while still generating pressure. The Steelers need those strikes to supplement an offense that has had uneven stretches sustaining possessions.

things.title: JUDKINS AND WARREN SET THE EARLY-DOWN TONE
things.body: Both teams have productive running backs in Quinshon Judkins and Jaylen Warren, but neither wants to spend the afternoon facing predictable third-and-long. Cleveland can protect Watson by gaining useful yards on first down; Pittsburgh can ease Rodgers' workload by finding Warren touches before the Browns' front gets upfield.

breakdown.bottom_line: Their first meeting swung from a Cleveland second-quarter surge to a Pittsburgh fourth-quarter comeback, then one decisive field goal. This rematch has similar margins: whichever front controls early downs and protects its quarterback will dictate the pace. Turnover avoidance and red-zone finishing matter more here than raw yardage, especially if the teams trade long possessions into the fourth.
